## Summary

Adds an opt-in `--enable-request-stats-headers` flag that attaches per-request timing and token-count headers to non-streaming OpenAI responses (chat, completion, responses):

```
x-vllm-total-time, x-vllm-queue-time, x-vllm-prefill-time,
x-vllm-decode-time, x-vllm-inference-time,
x-vllm-prompt-tokens, x-vllm-completion-tokens,
x-vllm-cached-tokens, x-vllm-time-per-output-token
```

**Single source of truth.** Timing intervals are computed in one place — `compute_timing_intervals` in `vllm/v1/metrics/stats.py` — and consumed by both the existing Prometheus path (`FinishedRequestStats`) and the new headers middleware. The middleware does no arithmetic, only formatting.

**Headers, not body.** Timings go in HTTP headers rather than the response body, so the OpenAI response schema is unchanged and strict client validators need no updates.

**Transport.** The finished-request stats reach the header middleware via a private attribute (`RequestResponseMetadata._finished_stats`) already stored on `request.state`. It is not a validated Pydantic field, so it stays out of schema introspection — no `arbitrary_types_allowed`, no cross-module import into `protocol.py`, and `FinishReason` needs no relocation.

**Streaming and errors unchanged.** The middleware is a no-op when `_finished_stats` is absent, which covers streaming (no terminal `RequestOutput`), errors, and non-OpenAI routes.

**n>1 and multi-prompt.** Headers describe a single generation stream, so they are suppressed for `n>1` and multi-prompt batch requests (stats belong to only one sequence) — consistent across chat and completion.

## Why this isn't a duplicate

- **Supersedes #38572** (also mine) — same feature, but that version recomputed the timing intervals inside the middleware instead of reusing `FinishedRequestStats`. Closed in favor of this one.
- **Different from #36383** (draft) — that adds a `metrics` field to the response *body* and bundles a `reasoning_tokens` change. This PR is headers-only, no body-schema change. The two can coexist.

## Test Plan

```bash
# Unit + middleware tests (no GPU)
uv run --no-sync python -m pytest \
    tests/entrypoints/openai/test_request_stats_headers.py \
    tests/v1/metrics/test_stats.py -v

# Live smoke test
vllm serve facebook/opt-125m --enable-request-stats-headers --port 8000
curl -is http://localhost:8000/v1/completions \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d '{"model":"facebook/opt-125m","prompt":"Hello","max_tokens":10}' \
    | grep -i '^x-vllm-'
```

**Manual verification (Linux + CUDA):**
- All 9 `x-vllm-*` headers present on non-streaming responses; values internally consistent (`prefill + decode ≈ inference`).
- Streaming requests confirmed to emit no `x-vllm-*` headers.
- Server started without the flag emits no headers.
- Prefix-cache hits (`x-vllm-cached-tokens > 0`) confirmed on repeated prompts.

## Test Results

- Header/middleware and metrics unit tests pass locally; import-cycle smoke test confirms `vllm.v1.metrics.stats` and `vllm.v1.engine` load without circularity.
- `pre-commit` clean on touched files (ruff check, ruff format, mypy, SPDX).

Just a question: what benefits of receiving the per-requests stats via custom response headers over collecting via distributed tracing? There already are so-called AI gateways ([smg](https://github.com/lightseekorg/smg), [envoy AI gateway](https://github.com/envoyproxy/ai-gateway), [litellm proxy](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm) to name a few) whose whole purpose is to collect the per-request stats and transform into a [business-standard](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/gen-ai/gen-ai-events/) trace protocols, and vllm integrates well with these. Is there a specific usecase where distributed tracing does not cover well?

@cjackal Thanks for the interest in the PR!

So I am aware of a use-case where we have OTel data available as spans and they can be queried using Grafana. I think the value in adding headers is based on the fact that this gives us an easy in-line access path, which opens up much more configurability for proxies that are being run in front of vLLM deployments.

In our use-case, we have our own internal implementation of an AI Gateway, where we want to implement latency aware load balancing and also have cost-based rate limiting based on the inference time taken by the request. Since e2e wall time bundles queue waiting into the same number as compute, it's the wrong basis for cost attribution when multiple teams share a model — they'd be charged for each other's queueing. Exposing the headers gives us the opportunity to calculate cost and make routing decisions inline, without going through an OTel pipeline lookup that carries span-export lag (typically several seconds before a finished request's span is queryable) and a separate per-request query to the trace backend. It also helps us return values like `per-request-cost` in real time without having to thread that through the OTel pipeline.

For cross-service spans, audit, post-hoc analysis, OTel is clearly the right tool. I would think this to be a complementary source of the same data, without it being a replacement. Hope this makes sense and happy to answer any questions further!

issue_comments.body: Just a question: what benefits of receiving the per-requests stats via custom response headers over collecting via distributed tracing? There already are so-called AI gateways ([smg](https://github.com/lightseekorg/smg), [envoy AI gateway](https://github.com/envoyproxy/ai-gateway), [litellm proxy](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm) to name a few) whose whole purpose is to collect the per-request stats and transform into a [business-standard](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/gen-ai/gen-ai-events/) trace protocols, and vllm integrates well with these. Is there a specific usecase where distributed tracing does not cover well?

@cjackal Thanks for the interest in the PR!

So I am aware of a use-case where we have OTel data available as spans and they can be queried using Grafana. I think the value in adding headers is based on the fact that this gives us an easy in-line access path, which opens up much more configurability for proxies that are being run in front of vLLM deployments.

In our use-case, we have our own internal implementation of an AI Gateway, where we want to implement latency aware load balancing and also have cost-based rate limiting based on the inference time taken by the request. Since e2e wall time bundles queue waiting into the same number as compute, it's the wrong basis for cost attribution when multiple teams share a model — they'd be charged for each other's queueing. Exposing the headers gives us the opportunity to calculate cost and make routing decisions inline, without going through an OTel pipeline lookup that carries span-export lag (typically several seconds before a finished request's span is queryable) and a separate per-request query to the trace backend. It also helps us return values like `per-request-cost` in real time without having to thread that through the OTel pipeline.

For cross-service spans, audit, post-hoc analysis, OTel is clearly the right tool. I would think this to be a complementary source of the same data, without it being a replacement. Hope this makes sense and happy to answer any questions further!
